title: Use Jev in AI agent loops: routing, checks and fallbacks
description: Place Jev at bounded agent decisions, batch independent checks, keep actions and permissions in code, and test full-task speed instead of trusting headline multiples.

faqs.question: Where should Jev sit in an AI agent loop?
faqs.answer: Put Jev at a repeated judgment with a known answer space, such as choosing an eligible route or checking a stated condition after a tool result. Keep planning and prose with an LLM, and keep permissions, actions, stop rules and outcome checks in code or human review.

faqs.question: Does Jev make an entire agent loop 200x faster?
faqs.answer: No such end-to-end result is established by Morlex's article. The headline draws on TypeSafe decision-workload evaluations and individual demos. Measure your full task, including LLM calls, tools, retries and review, before claiming a gain.

faqs.question: Can Jev decide whether a tool call is safe?
faqs.answer: It can supply a bounded risk judgment, but that judgment is not authorization. Code must still enforce permissions and hard rules, and a person must approve actions your policy reserves for human review.

faqs.question: What happens when Jev is uncertain or unavailable?
faqs.answer: Do not silently execute the proposed action. Send uncertain cases to the defined fallback or a person, and make a provider error visible so the loop can stop or use a reviewed safe path.

faqs.question: Is Jev Ultrafast required to use this pattern?
faqs.answer: No. Jev Ultrafast is a source-mentioned browser example, not a dependency of every Jev agent. Use it to study how a fresh action list, typed choice and independent outcome check fit together.
